title: What do strong market sizing answers look like across 24 worked examples?
description: Twenty-four market sizing questions, from coffee cups to hotel rooms, each with a step-by-step worked answer and sanity check.
hook: Strong market sizing answers all share the same shape: a clarified question, a rough guess, a short chain of round assumptions said out loud, a check from a second angle, and a rounded answer with the assumption that drives it. The 24 examples below, from coffee cups to hotel rooms, each show that shape in full. Try each one yourself before you open the worked answer.
body:
In this guide

  • How to use these examples
  • Good first questions
  • A step up
  • Harder ones
  • Five patterns that cover almost every question
  • What strong answers have in common
  • How to challenge your own estimate
  • Practice
  • Where to practise next

How to use these examples

If you have not yet read the step-by-step market sizing method, start there. Then work through these in order of difficulty. For each one:

  1. Read only the question. Give yourself two minutes and answer out loud, as you would in an interview.
  2. Open the worked answer and compare your structure, not your number. Did you clarify the same things? Did you pick the same side (buyers or sellers)? Did you check yourself?
  3. Note the one assumption that moved the answer most. That is the lesson of the question.

Your number will often differ by 20% or 30%. That is fine. Interviewers care far more about how you got there.

Good first questions

Short chains with inputs you can picture from daily life.

QuestionAnswerWhat it teaches
Cups of coffee London cafés sell on a weekdayAbout 3.5M cupsCount the adults actually in the city that day, including commuters
UK spending on umbrellas a yearAbout $280MA replacement market, checked by the stock in people's homes
Full-time wedding photographers the UK needsAbout 10kCapacity comes from editing time, not just Saturdays
Yearly revenue of one busy London coffee shopAbout $1MTest the morning peak, not the daily average
Car tyres sold in the UK a yearAbout 34M replacementsStock divided by life gives the yearly flow
Toothbrushes and heads Americans buy a yearAbout 800MAdvice is a ceiling; model real behaviour
UK cinema box office a yearAbout $1.2BVisits per person is the input to defend
Bottled water the UK drinks a yearAbout 3.4B litresHeavy users drive the average
Laptops UK university students buy a yearAbout 800kSize the buying moments: starting a course and replacing
Delivery pizzas the UK orders a weekAbout 7MKeep orders and pizzas apart
UK family spending on school uniforms a yearAbout $4BSegment primary and secondary pupils

A step up

More steps, more segmentation, or a supply-side twist.

QuestionAnswerWhat it teaches
Hairdressers working in LondonAbout 26k full-timeDemand divided by capacity, then convert to headcount
The US dog food marketAbout $40BBuild spend per dog from a bag of food, then segment by size
Smartphones sold in India a yearAbout 175MBig populations make the replacement cycle decisive
The UK gym membership marketAbout $6.7BA sanity check shows which assumption to revisit
Piano tuners in ChicagoAbout 70The classic demand-over-capacity chain
Parcels delivered to UK homes a yearAbout 2.6BBuild the weekly average from household types
Office chairs UK employers buy a yearAbout 1.6MHybrid working changes desks per worker
Yearly revenue of US car washesAbout $13BSplit pay-per-wash from memberships
Ride-hailing trips in London a dayAbout 450kA small daily share drives everything; check against drivers
Home EV chargers installed in the UK a yearAbout 220k a yearOff-street parking is the limiting factor

Harder ones

Several moving parts, or a unit conversion that is easy to get wrong.

QuestionAnswerWhat it teaches
Dentists the UK needsAbout 45kTreatment time, not check-ups, drives demand
Passengers using Heathrow a dayAbout 230kStart from flights, and allow for big long-haul jets
Hotel rooms in ParisAbout 90k roomsOccupancy and guests per room both belong in the maths

Five patterns that cover almost every question

Most sizing questions are one of five shapes. Recognising the shape in the first ten seconds tells you the formula.

1. Population chain

Population × share in segment × share who buy × frequency × price. Coffee cups, cinema, dog food, gyms. The skill is choosing the right base: adults, households or the people actually present (as with London's commuters).

2. Replacement cycle

Things in use ÷ years they last. Tyres, umbrellas, phones, office chairs. The skill is separating the stock (in use) from the flow (bought per year), then naming the life assumption as the sensitive one.

3. Demand over capacity

Work needed ÷ work one person can do. Hairdressers, piano tuners, wedding photographers, dentists. The skill is building capacity from a realistic working year, then converting full-time equivalents into headcount if asked.

4. Single business

Customers a day × spend × trading days. The busy coffee shop. The skill is testing the busiest hour, not the average one.

5. Supply-side count

Units of supply × throughput. Heathrow (flights × seats × load factor), hotel rooms. Use it when sellers are few and countable, or when buyer behaviour is hard to picture.

What strong answers have in common

Across all 24, the strong answer sounds like this:

"I'll size this from buyers and check it against sellers. [Three or four assumptions, each with a reason.] That gives about X. The other side gives a similar number. The assumption that moves this most is Y, so that's what I'd want to test."

The weak answer sounds like this:

"68 million people times a third times ten is 226.7 million."

Same multiplication, but no clarification, no reasons, false precision and no check. The interviewer learns nothing about your judgement.

How to challenge your own estimate

Take the office chairs example. Suppose you estimate that about 12M desk chairs are in use and each lasts eight years, giving 12M ÷ 8 = 1.5M replacement chairs a year. Before you call it done, run three checks:

  • Definition. Have you counted replacements only, or new desks too? Growing employers and new offices add purchases; hybrid working and second-hand chairs reduce them.
  • Stock and flow. Chairs in offices are a stock. Chairs bought this year are a flow. Make sure your answer is the one the question asked for.
  • Sensitivity. Vary the most uncertain input. If chairs last six years instead of eight, demand becomes 12M ÷ 6 = 2.0M, a third higher.

A strong finish often gives a range: "On these assumptions, about 1.5 to 2 million chairs a year, depending mainly on how long a chair lasts." The reasoning is what makes the number defensible.

Practice

Two new questions, not covered above. Answer out loud before you look.

1. How many dishwashers are sold in the UK each year?

Show the answer

Replacement cycle. About 28M households; assume half own a dishwasher, so 14M in use. If one lasts about ten years, replacements are 14M ÷ 10 = 1.4M a year. First-time buyers add a little. Check: that is one new dishwasher for every 20 households a year, which feels plausible.

2. How many cups of tea does the UK drink each day?

Show the answer

Population chain. About 55M adults; assume 60% drink tea, 3 cups a day each: 55M × 60% × 3 = 99M, so about 100M cups a day. Check: that is about 1.5 cups for every person in the UK, children included, which fits a tea-drinking country.

Where to practise next

Read what to ask first in a market sizing case for the short routine, and learn the numbers worth knowing by heart so your starting inputs are quick. For timed reps with model answers, use the market sizing drill, and when you are ready for a full case, try Plugged In or BrightStep Tutoring in the casebook.
